column1: # boru Language Specification: the boru:io module
# Format: input<TAB>expected<TAB>description
# Loadable module of input/output words that were moved out of the core
# registry. Most are reached only after `import`, under the `IO`
# namespace: `import "boru:io" IO.word args`. `print` is NOT here — it
# stays a core word so basic output needs no import.
# FILE I/O IS PATHON-ONLY. Every filesystem target is a `Scalar/Micron/
# Pathon` built with `make Pathon "…"` — a bare string is declined, so a
# file target is type-distinct from an arbitrary string and from a stream
# handle. A word that returns its target returns that Pathon (rendered
# without quotes), so `IO.read (IO.write p x)` threads through.
# `list` and `remove` are the exception to the namespace rule: boru:io
# extends the CORE `list` / `remove` words with a Pathon overload, so
# after import the BARE words gain filesystem behaviour — `list p` /
# `remove p` — rather than a separate `IO.list` / `IO.remove` (see
# design/OPEN-WORDS.0.md). The overload only registers on import.
# §1  stream handles — `stdin`/`stdout`/`stderr` are ATOMs of the
#     StreamKind type (a closed enumeration of exactly those three, not
#     strings). StreamKind is exported by this module — `IO.StreamKind`,
#     not a global builtin.
import "boru:io" IO.stdout
column3: standard-output handle is the `stdout` atom

column1: import "boru:io" IO.stderr
column3: standard-error handle is the `stderr` atom

column3: a stream handle's type is StreamKind

column1: # §5  read / write against an in-memory filesystem
#     `context get __sys get fs set mem true` switches the FileOps capability
#     to an in-memory backing, so write-then-read is deterministic here.
#     `make Pathon "mem://b.txt"` collapses to the Pathon `mem:/b.txt`.
import "boru:io"  context dot __sys dot fs set mem true  IO.write (make Pathon "mem://b.txt") "hi"
column3: write returns the Pathon it wrote

column1: import "boru:io"  context dot __sys dot fs set mem true  IO.read (IO.write (make Pathon "mem://a.txt") "hello")
column3: read back the bytes just written

column1: # §6  writing NON-STRING data needs no options map, reading a stream that is
#     not stdin errors, and StreamKind-tagged write returns the handle — all
#     runtime behaviours exercised in lang/go/native/io_stream_test.go and
#     fileio_test.go (they return Any / raise runtime-only errors, which do
#     not belong on the static-checker spec surface).
# §8  stat — describe a Pathon, returning a FileInfo record (name/path/type/
#     size/mode/mtime, plus target for a symlink), or `none` when absent.
#     `type` is an IO.FileType atom (file/dir/symlink/other).
import "boru:io"  context dot __sys dot fs set mem true  IO.write (make Pathon "mem://s.txt") "hello" drop  (IO.stat (make Pathon "mem://s.txt")).size
column3: stat reports a file's byte size

#      Owner VALUES are environment-dependent (the process identity), so
#      the rows assert shape, not numbers.

#      A bare word after import, not IO.remove.

#      truncate, perm}. A handle shares the mem backing store, so a handle
#      write is visible to a stateless read before close.
import "boru:io"  context dot __sys dot fs set mem true  IO.write (make Pathon "mem://k") "x" drop  (IO.open (make Pathon "mem://k")) is IO.File

column1: # §28  read-line / tty — the filter-program surface. `IO.read-line` yields
#      the next line of a stream or File handle WITHOUT its terminator, or
#      none at EOF; `IO.is-tty` reports whether a stream is a terminal.
#      The rows below use a FILE HANDLE over the in-memory filesystem,
#      because stdin is not hermetic here: the spec runner never sets
#      Registry.Input, so it defaults to the real process stdin
#      (eng/go/registry.go:1167) and a stdin row would read whatever the
#      harness was launched with. The stdin arms — and the interaction with
#      `IO.read (IO.stdin)`, which shares one reader — are pinned in
#      lang/go/test/io_lines_test.go.
#      `IO.is-tty` answers FALSE here because the spec runner installs no
#      StreamProbe. That is the capability contract, not an accident: the
#      runtime never asks the OS what it is attached to unless a host hands
#      over a probe. The TRUE arm needs the fake, so it is a Go test too.
#      The word is `tty`, not the `tty?` of design/CLI-PROGRAMS.0.md §5:
#      `?` is a fixed lexer token, so `tty?` cannot be dispatched at all.
